incidents.para_title: How does Steinbeck use the incident of the mouse?
incidents.para: Lennie's obsession with petting soft things (mice, puppies and eventually Curley's wife's hair) is used by Steinbeck to highlight his childlike innocence, but it is, as we will see, this habit that leads to accidental violence, with him confessing that with the animals he pinched their heads then "they was dead, because they was so little." This highlights a tragic disconnect between intention and consequence; like an animal that doesn't know its own strength, Lennie kills it without meaning to. He treats mice and dogs like toys, but his lack of control, both physical and mental, turns these reactions deadly.

incidents.title: The Sacramento River
incidents.what: George admits that he once told Lennie to jump into the Sacramento River, even though Lennie couldn't swim.
notes: Knew that he would put Lennie in danger, but didn't care [p.12]
incidents.para: In Chapter 3, George has a conversation with Slim and confesses that he "used to play jokes" on Lennie and that he had once made Lennie [jump] into the Sacramento River, even with the fact George knew Lennie couldn't swim. Steinbeck uses this to show George's early immaturity and shows Lennie follows all orders from George like a father and son would. Over time George stops using his power on Lennie as he realises, after Lennie's near-death experience, that he has a duty to look after Lennie, so won't treat him that way again.

incidents.title: The Shooting of Candy's Dog
incidents.what: Carlson pressures Candy into letting him take the old dog outside and shoot it.
notes: When the dog was shot, Candy "turned to the wall" [p.16]
Had the dog "since he was a pup" [p.16]
incidents.para: In Chapter 3 of Of Mice and Men, Steinbeck's portrayal of Carlson's unceremonious shooting of Candy's dog is used to highlight the brutal pragmatism of ranch life and the dehumanising effects of the Great Depression and the hardships it produced. The dog is described as "old"; language which reduces it to a burden rather than a companion, reflecting a society that values usefulness over emotional connection. Carlson's insistence that the dog should be shot emphasises the cold, utilitarian mindset. Carlson lists all the things the dog "can't" do, but fails to see what it can do. The lack of ceremony in the killing, being done "offstage" as it were, with the "shot" breaking the bunkhouse silence. Candy's acquiescence reveals his awareness that he, too, is ageing, foreshadowing the fear of being cast aside when he is no longer of use.

incidents.title: Curley's Hand
incidents.what: Curley attacks Lennie in the bunkhouse; Lennie doesn't fight back until George tells him to.
notes: Lennie crushes Curley's hand once George tells him to defend himself. This incident is used by Steinbeck to foreshadow the danger Lennie poses when panicked or provoked [p.24]

paragraphs.title: How Steinbeck Introduces Curley
paragraphs.text: Steinbeck introduces Curley as an aggressive, insecure figure who relies on a strong posture to convey his apparent strength and dominance. Upon meeting the two men, Curley immediately shifts into a fighting stance, with his "hands closed into fists." This tense and angry reaction shows his hostility towards the men due to the fact he feels threatened by the larger men. It is interesting to note "his high-heeled boots" which signifies a desire to elevate his posture and the desire to stop being a "small guy" and to show off his authority. As well as this, when George meets the "pugnacious" Curley for the first time, George refers to Curley as a "punk", suggesting that he knows straight away that he is going to cause problems.

paragraphs.title: How Steinbeck Introduces Curley's Wife
paragraphs.text: Steinbeck introduces Curley's wife as an isolated person. When she is first in the bunkhouse, she stands in the "doorway", which portrays her as a threat to the men as she is standing over them. She is wearing "red," which is a clear contrast to the brown "whitewashed" bunkhouse. This shows her clear difference to the men and emphasises that people with authority (Curley, his wife and the boss) wear clothes to show their power. It is also interesting to note that Curley's wife is only referred to as "Curley's wife"; her name is not known. This and also the apostrophe on "Curley's" conveys the fact (due to the context of 1930s America) that Curley is the possessor of his wife and how she can be viewed as an object who can be owned.

feedback.target: When a word starts with a vowel, remember to use "an" — e.g. an isolated person, an apple, a chicken.

paragraphs.title: How Steinbeck Presents the Boss
paragraphs.text: The boss owns the land and controls the workers' jobs. This power makes him intimidating to the men and Steinbeck describes his flamboyant clothes to show his authority, such as the "square steel buckle" on his belt. Due to owning the land, the boss doesn't have to do "labor" or do manual work, which is suggested by his "high-heeled boots and spurs"; owning land gives him power to choose what he does and is a clear indication of why George and Lennie fixate upon owning "a little piece of land" themselves. Interestingly, we see the Boss is suspicious of George. We hear him ask "Say, what you selling?" and "What stake you got in this guy?" Steinbeck uses the Boss here to present a world where kindness and loyalty are unusual, causing people to distrust the friendship. The word "selling" implies deceit, as though George is trying to gain something from Lennie rather than simply helping him.

paragraphs.title: Embedding: George's "Own Crops"
paragraphs.text: We hear George, when confessing to Slim, suggest that "if I was bright" he would have his "own crops" instead of working for someone in a higher echelon. George implies that people at the bottom do the work but don't get the fruits of their labour. This highlights the injustice of a system which is exploitative.
